# Unclaimed

The umbrellas come first, always. By the second week of November the bin behind my desk is bristling like a hedgehog, black canopies and plaid, one made of clear plastic with daisies printed along the seam. Nobody comes back for umbrellas. An umbrella is the only possession a person will abandon mid-storm and replace within the hour, and I have stopped taking it personally.

I work at the lost property office of Central Station. Twenty-two years. People imagine romance — reunions, tears, a violin returned to a weeping student. Mostly it's phones. Phones, umbrellas, gloves in tragic singles. The gloves bother me more than they should. Somewhere in this city there are drawers full of lone gloves, each waiting for a partner that got off at a different stop.

The office smells of cold radiator and old wool. Trains announce themselves through the wall in a language of chimes. Between four and six the queue runs long — a boy who left his grandfather's medal on the 6:40, a bride whose dress bag vanished between taxis — and I stamp forms and listen, because listening is half of it. Everyone who stands at this counter is really asking one question: does the world keep what we drop?

We hold everything for ninety days. Then books go to the library sale, clothes to charity, electronics to a recycler who strips them for gold. I log each item in a ledger my supervisor calls obsolete and I call insurance. Serial number, description, date found, date claimed or destroyed. In twenty-two years I have written perhaps nine thousand entries. Some of them I remember better than my own birthdays.

Item 4471: a man's wristwatch, stopped at 4:17, engraved *To Harold — all my love, always*. Unclaimed. Item 5102: a shoebox of letters tied with green ribbon, postmarked 1963 through 1971, every envelope addressed in the same careful hand. Unclaimed. Item 6888: a single hearing aid, beige, still faintly warm when it came in, as though the ear had only just let it go. Unclaimed. I checked the batteries on that one. They were fine. It was working. It was simply no longer being heard.

People ask if I read the letters. I used to say no. The truth is I read the first lines only, enough to know whether the contents are dangerous — keys to safes, medical results, anything that would oblige me to make phone calls. But first lines are worse than whole letters. *Dear Ruth, I have thought about how to begin this for six weeks.* Nothing follows that beginning except a life.

There is a shelf under the window where I keep the things I cannot send away. Not stolen — reassigned. A brass compass whose needle points confidently in the wrong direction. A photograph of three women laughing on a pier, salt damage eating their dresses, their faces untouched. A child's drawing of a house with too many windows, signed *Madison, age 6*, rendered in crayon so hard the paper tore. When the auditors come I tell them these are pending claims. Twenty-two years of pending. No one has ever opened the drawer twice.

People assume I'm sentimental. I'm not, particularly. I lost things long before I took this job — a red scarf on a night bus in 1991, my father's fountain pen in a taxi I couldn't name afterward. I know how it feels to stand at a counter like mine and hear the kind voice say *nothing has come in yet*. Nothing has come in yet. Those five words are why the shelf exists.

Once — this was maybe eight years ago — a woman came in asking about a handbag lost in 1984. I explained gently that our records went back only to 1999, that the office had been across the concourse then, near the flower stand. She nodded as if I'd confirmed something rather than failed her. *I remember exactly what it looked like,* she said. Navy leather. A gold clasp shaped like a swallow. Her mother bought it for her the week she found out she was pregnant. She stood there a moment, hands folded, doing arithmetic with the years. Then she said, *Thank you for keeping the room,* and left. I have thought about that phrase more than any inventory entry. Keeping the room. As though the office itself were the service — a place where losing is allowed to stay official for ninety days before it becomes permanent.

Here is what twenty-two years has taught me: almost nothing is lost on purpose. The wedding ring left on the sink edge of the ladies' room belonged to a hand that had been holding it while it washed, the way you do, absent, thinking of something else. The ashes — yes, we had ashes once, item 7730, a walnut urn the size of a teapot — were set down by a son who stopped to check the departure board and simply walked into his new life without his father. He came back on day eighty-eight. He wept in my office and thanked me as if I'd done something, and I said the true thing, which is that I hadn't done anything. I had only refused to throw him away.

Refusal is most of the job. Anyone can store a suitcase. The work is in the last week of the ninety days, when the shelves get crowded and the ledger waits and every unclaimed thing asks to be called junk so the throwing away can feel like tidiness. I resist. I move slowly. I am, I admit, a bureaucrat of hesitation.

Some nights, locking up, I look down the rows of shelving — the suitcases with their airline tags gone soft as moth wings, the guitars in their cases like closed coffins, the bin of umbrellas drying out for another year — and I think about how every object here is a promise somebody made and forgot. *Come back for me. I'll be here.* And the station roars above us, ten thousand people a day losing gloves and phones and fathers, and below, in the fluorescent hush, everything waits, catalogued and patient, certain in the way only abandoned things are certain that someone is coming.

My job is to keep the promise anyway.

2. An essay/reflection
3. A prose poem
4. Something experimental

Since it's "whatever comes to you," I could lean into something that feels spontaneous but crafted. A short story with a strong voice might be best. Or a lyrical essay about something unexpected — like the interior life of a lighthouse keeper, or a meditation on a specific small thing.

- The last day of a small-town movie theater

- A woman who keeps her late husband's voicemail by never letting the phone battery die... wait, that's a known concept (people preserving voicemails). Could still be done freshly.
- A cartographer drawing maps of places that no longer exist
- Someone who works at a lost-and-found office and the objects' stories

I like the lost-and-found idea or the translator one. Or maybe something more meditative: an essay on waiting rooms? On the color of late afternoon light?

Alternative: write in second person? That can feel gimmicky. First person past tense is safe; present tense can feel immediate.

**Unclaimed**

The umbrellas come first, always. By the second week of November the bin behind my desk is bristling like a hedgehog, black canopies and plaid, one made of clear plastic with daisies printed along the seam. Nobody comes back for umbrellas. An umbrella is the only possession a person will abandon mid-storm and replace within the hour, and I have stopped taking it personally.

I work at the lost property office of Central Station. Twenty-two years. People imagine romance — reunions, tears, a violin returned to a weeping student. Mostly it's phones. Phones, umbrellas, gloves in tragic singles. The gloves bother me more than they should. Somewhere in this city there are drawers full of lone gloves, each waiting for a partner that got off at a different stop.

We hold everything for ninety days. Then books go to the library sale, clothes to charity, electronics to a recycler who strips them for gold. I log each item in a ledger my supervisor calls obsolete and I call insurance. Serial number, description, date found, date claimed or destroyed. In twenty-two years I have written perhaps nine thousand entries. Some of them I remember better than my own birthdays.

Item 4471: a man's wristwatch, stopped at 4:17, engraved To Harold — all my love, always. Unclaimed. Item 5102: a shoebox of letters tied with green ribbon, postmarked 1963 through 1971, every envelope addressed in the same careful hand. Unclaimed. Item 6888: a single hearing aid, beige, still faintly warm when it came in, as though the ear had only just let it go. Unclaimed. I checked the batteries on that one. They were fine. It was working. It was simply no longer being heard.

People ask if I read the letters. I used to say no. The truth is I read the first lines only, enough to know whether the contents are dangerous — keys to safes, medical results, anything that would oblige me to make phone calls. But first lines are worse than whole letters. Dear Ruth, I have thought about how to begin this for six weeks. Nothing follows that beginning except a life.

There is a shelf under the window where I keep the things I cannot send away. Not stolen — reassigned. A brass compass whose needle points confidently in the wrong direction. A photograph of three women laughing on a pier, salt damage eating their dresses, their faces untouched. A child's drawing of a house with too many windows, signed Madison, age 6, rendered in crayon so hard the paper tore. When the auditors come I tell them these are pending claims. Twenty-two years of pending. No one has ever opened the drawer twice.

Once — this was maybe eight years ago — a woman came in asking about a handbag lost in 1984. I explained gently that our records went back only to 1999, that the office had been across the concourse then, near the flower stand. She nodded as if I'd confirmed something rather than failed her. I remember exactly what it looked like, she said. Navy leather. A gold clasp shaped like a swallow. My mother bought it for me the week I found out I was pregnant. She stood there a moment, hands folded, doing arithmetic with the years. Then she said, Thank you for keeping the room, and left. I have thought about that phrase more than any inventory entry. Keeping the room. As though the office itself were the service — a place where losing is allowed to remain official for ninety days before it becomes permanent.

Here is what twenty-two years has taught me: almost nothing is lost on purpose. The wedding ring left on the sink edge of the ladies' room belonged to a hand that had been holding it while it washed, the way you do, absent, thinking of something else. The ashes — yes, we had ashes once, item 7730, a walnut urn the size of a teapot — were set down by a son who stopped to check the departure board and simply walked into his new life without his father. He came back on day eighty-eight. He wept in my office and thanked me as if I'd done something, and I said the true thing, which is that I hadn't done anything, I had only refused to throw him away.

Refusal is most of the job. Anyone can store a suitcase. The work is in the last week of the ninety days, when the shelf gets crowded and the ledger waits and every unclaimed thing asks to be called junk so the throwing away can feel like tidiness. I resist. I move slowly. I am, I admit, a bureaucrat of hesitation.

Some nights, locking up, I look down the rows of shelving — the suitcases with their airline tags soft as moth wings, the guitars in their cases like closed coffins, the bin of umbrellas drying out for another year — and I think about how every object here is a promise somebody made and forgot. Come back for me. I'll be here. And the station roars above us, ten thousand people a day losing gloves and phones and fathers, and below, in the fluorescent hush, everything waits, catalogued and patient, certain in the way only abandoned things are certain that someone is coming.

My job is to keep the promise anyway.
